title: Running a Business Online
tagline: Reach more customers, sell safely and keep simple records.
description: Whether you sell vegetables, tailor clothes or run a salon, your phone can bring you more customers. This course shows you how to set up a business profile, take good product photos, talk to customers, take payments safely and keep simple records that show if you are making a profit.
outcomes: Set up a WhatsApp Business profile and catalogue
Create a Facebook page for your business
Know the basics of registering a business in Zambia
Take clear product photos and write good posts
Keep simple records and know your profit

modules.title: Getting set up
modules.summary: Your business profile, a Facebook page and registration basics.

lessons.title: Setting up a WhatsApp Business profile
lessons.body:
**WhatsApp Business** is a free app made for small businesses. It looks like normal WhatsApp but adds tools that make you look professional and save time.

## Getting started
1. Install **WhatsApp Business** from the Play Store.
2. Register with the number you want customers to use. Many owners use a separate SIM for business, so family chats stay apart.
3. Enter your **business name** exactly as customers know it.

## Fill in your profile
Tap the three dots, **Settings**, then **Business tools**, then **Business profile**:

- **Category:** for example *Clothing store* or *Beauty salon*.
- **Description:** one or two lines, like *Fresh vegetables from our farm. Delivery in Kabwe town.*
- **Address** or area, and **opening hours**.
- A clear **profile photo**: your logo, shop front or best product.

## Time-saving tools
- **Greeting message:** sent automatically to new customers. *"Thank you for contacting Mama Bwalya Tailoring. How can we help?"*
- **Away message:** sent when you are closed.
- **Quick replies:** save answers you type often, like prices or directions. Type / to use them.
- **Labels:** mark chats as *New order*, *Paid*, *Delivered*.

## Catalogue
Under **Catalogue**, add your products with a photo, price and short description. Customers can browse without asking you for every price.
key_points: WhatsApp Business is free and made for small businesses
Fill in category, description, hours and photo
Use greeting messages, quick replies and a catalogue
lessons.try_it: Install WhatsApp Business and write your business description.

lessons.title: Creating a Facebook page
lessons.body:
A **Facebook page** is separate from your personal profile. It lets people find and follow your business without seeing your private life.

## Creating the page
1. In the Facebook app, tap the menu, then **Pages**, then **Create**.
2. Enter your business name and choose a category.
3. Add a short description with what you sell and where.
4. Add a **profile picture** (logo or best product) and a **cover photo** (your shop, products or team).
5. Add your phone number, WhatsApp and location.

## Invite your first followers
Invite your friends to like the page, and ask happy customers to follow it. Share the page link on your WhatsApp status.

## What to post
- New stock and prices.
- Photos of your best work.
- Customer reviews, with their permission.
- Opening hours, holidays and special offers.

Post regularly, two or three times a week, so people remember you. Posting at times when people are free, like lunchtime and evening, gets more views.

## Messages and reviews
Reply to messages quickly and politely, even just to say you will get back to them. Answer questions in comments in public, so others see the answer too. If someone complains, reply calmly and offer to sort it out by message.

## Marketplace
Facebook **Marketplace** lets you list items for people nearby to see. It is useful for one-off items and second-hand goods.
key_points: A page keeps business separate from your personal profile
Post two or three times a week
Reply to messages and comments quickly and politely
lessons.try_it: Write the description you would use for your business page.

lessons.title: Registering your business: the basics
lessons.body:
You can sell without registering when you are very small. But registering makes your business official. It helps you open a business bank account, get contracts with bigger companies, apply for loans and grants, and protect your business name.

## Business name registration
In Zambia, business names and companies are registered with **PACRA** (the Patents and Companies Registration Agency). A small business owned by one person is often registered as a **business name**.

The usual steps are:
1. **Name clearance:** check that the name you want is available.
2. **Registration:** fill in the form and pay the fee.

You can do this at a PACRA office or online through the government's **e-services portal** (eservices.gov.zm, linked from ZamPortal), where you fill in forms, pay and receive results.

## Tax
The **Zambia Revenue Authority (ZRA)** handles tax. Businesses need a **TPIN** (Taxpayer Identification Number). Small businesses may be able to use simpler tax arrangements, such as turnover tax. Rules, rates and limits change, so ask ZRA directly or visit their official website for the current rules.

## Local permits
Your **local council** may require a trading licence or permit, depending on your business and where you trade. Ask at the council offices.

## Get advice
Fees and rules change. Check the official PACRA, ZRA and council information, or ask a business support organisation or ICT hub to help you through it. Be careful of people online who offer to "register you quickly" for a fee, and only deal with official offices.
key_points: PACRA registers business names and companies
ZRA issues the TPIN and explains tax rules
Check official sources, as fees and rules change
lessons.try_it: Think of a name for your business and check it is not already used by searching online.

modules.title: Showing and selling
modules.summary: Photos, posts and talking to customers.

lessons.title: Taking good product photos
lessons.body:
Customers decide in a second whether to look closer. A clear photo sells better than a long description.

## Light
- Use **daylight**. Stand near a window or work outside in the shade.
- Avoid harsh midday sun, which makes dark shadows.
- Turn off the flash. It makes products look flat and shiny.

## Background
- Use a **plain background**: a clean wall, a white sheet or a piece of chitenge with a simple pattern.
- Remove clutter, like bags, cups and other items.

## Showing the product
- Fill most of the picture with the product.
- Take several photos: the front, the back, a close-up of detail, and the product in use. A dress worn by a person, a cake on a plate.
- Show the **size**. Put a common object next to it, or write the measurements.
- Show the **real colour**. Do not use filters that change it, or customers will be disappointed.

## Steady and sharp
- Hold the phone with two hands, or rest it on something.
- Tap the screen on the product to focus before you take the picture.
- Clean the camera lens with a soft cloth. A dirty lens makes everything blurry.

## Keep it honest
Only show photos of what you are really selling. Using pictures from the internet loses customers' trust when the real item looks different.
key_points: Daylight and a plain background
Take several angles and show the size
Tap to focus and clean your lens
lessons.try_it: Take three photos of one product using daylight and a plain background. Pick the best one.

lessons.title: Writing posts customers understand
lessons.body:
A good post tells customers what you sell, what it costs and how to buy it, quickly and clearly.

## The four things every post needs
1. **What it is:** *Ladies' chitenge dresses, sizes 10 to 18.*
2. **The price:** *K250 each.* Posts with prices get more serious enquiries.
3. **Why it is good:** *Made to measure in 3 days. Strong stitching.*
4. **How to buy:** *WhatsApp 097... or visit us at stand 12, Chisokone Market.*

## Keep it short
Most people read posts on small screens while busy. Use short sentences and put the most important thing first.

## Use the right language
Write in the language your customers use. A mix of English and a local language is fine if that is how your customers speak.

## Status updates
Your **WhatsApp status** is seen by everyone who has saved your number. Post new stock, offers and finished work there every day or two. It is free advertising.

## Honest offers
If you announce a discount, keep to it. Write when it ends: *Offer ends Saturday.* Do not make claims you cannot prove, like *best in Zambia*.

## Hashtags and location
On Facebook and Instagram, adding your town and simple hashtags like #Kitwe or #ZambianFashion helps nearby people find you.

## Ask happy customers
A short message from a happy customer, shared with their permission, is more convincing than anything you write yourself.
key_points: What it is, the price, why it is good, how to buy
Short sentences, most important first
Use your WhatsApp status as free advertising
lessons.try_it: Write one post for a product with all four parts.

lessons.title: Talking to customers online
lessons.body:
Good service online brings customers back and makes them recommend you.

## Reply quickly
Customers often ask several sellers at once. The first good reply usually wins. If you are busy, send a quick reply: *"Thank you! I will send the prices in 30 minutes."* Your WhatsApp Business **quick replies** help here.

## Be clear
- Confirm the **item, size or colour, quantity, price and delivery** in one message before the customer pays.
- Give a realistic time: *Ready on Thursday after 2 pm.*
- If something changes, tell the customer early.

## Be polite, even when it is hard
- Greet customers and thank them.
- Do not argue in public comments. Move difficult conversations to private messages.
- If you made a mistake, say sorry and offer a fair fix: a replacement, a repair or a refund.

## Handling complaints
1. Listen to the full complaint.
2. Thank them for telling you.
3. Ask for a photo if it helps.
4. Offer a solution and do what you promise.

A complaint handled well can turn an unhappy customer into a loyal one.

## Respect privacy
Do not share customers' numbers, addresses or photos without permission. Do not add them to groups without asking. Customer information is a responsibility, and Zambia has a data protection law about it.

## Follow up
A short message a few days later, *"Is the dress fitting well?"*, shows you care and invites repeat orders.
key_points: Reply quickly, even just to say you will answer soon
Confirm item, price and delivery before payment
Handle complaints calmly and keep your promises
lessons.try_it: Save three quick replies in WhatsApp Business: a greeting, your prices and your location.

modules.title: Payments and records
modules.summary: Safe payments, delivery and knowing your profit.

lessons.title: Taking payments safely
lessons.body:
Mobile money makes it easy for customers to pay you. A few habits protect you from tricks.

## Use a merchant or till number if you can
Networks offer **merchant accounts** or till numbers for businesses. They show your business name to customers, and keep business money separate from your personal wallet. Ask your network about the options and fees.

## Check payments in your menu, not just the SMS
Before you hand over goods:
1. Open your mobile money menu and check your **balance** or **mini statement**.
2. Confirm the amount and the sender's name.

Scammers send **fake payment SMS messages** from normal phone numbers that look like real ones. Your balance is the truth.

## The overpayment trick
A "customer" pays more than the price, then asks you to send back the difference. Often the first payment was fake or will be reversed. Do not send money back. Say they should contact their network to reverse it.

## Deposits for custom orders
For made-to-order work, like a tailored outfit or a cake, ask for a **deposit** before you buy materials. Write down what was agreed and send it to the customer.

## Cash
- Count cash in front of the customer.
- Learn to recognise genuine kwacha notes.
- Do not keep large amounts of cash in your stall. Deposit it into mobile money or the bank regularly.

## Receipts
Send a simple receipt by WhatsApp: date, item, amount, and *Paid, thank you.* It builds trust and helps your records.
key_points: Check your balance before handing over goods
Do not send back 'overpayments'
Take deposits for custom orders
lessons.try_it: Ask your network what merchant or till options they have for small businesses.

lessons.title: Delivery and building trust
lessons.body:
Selling online means customers cannot touch the product before they pay, and you cannot see the customer. Trust works both ways.

## Delivery options
- **Pick-up:** the customer collects from your shop or stall.
- **Your own delivery:** you or a helper delivers within your area. Agree the delivery fee before.
- **Bus or courier parcels** for other towns. Keep the receipt and tracking details, and send a photo of the parcel and receipt to the customer.

## Meeting safely
If you meet customers to hand over goods:

- Meet in a **busy public place**, like a shopping centre or outside a bank, in daylight.
- Tell someone where you are going.
- Do not hand over goods until payment is confirmed in your mobile money menu.

## Payment on delivery
Cash on delivery reduces the customer's risk, but increases yours. For new customers, ask for a small deposit first, or use payment on collection at a public place.

## Building trust
- Use your **real business name**, the same on WhatsApp, Facebook and your stall.
- Share **reviews** and photos from happy customers, with permission.
- Have a clear **return or exchange rule**, like *exchange within 3 days if unused*. Write it in your profile.
- Keep your promises on time and quality.

## When things go wrong
If an item is damaged in delivery, talk to the customer calmly and fix it fairly. How you handle problems is what people remember.
key_points: Meet in busy public places in daylight
Confirm payment before handing over goods
A clear return rule and real reviews build trust
lessons.try_it: Write a short return or exchange rule for your business.

lessons.title: Keeping simple records and knowing your profit
lessons.body:
Many businesses look busy but do not make money. **Records** show you the truth.

## Sales minus costs
**Profit = money from sales minus all your costs.**

Costs include stock, materials, transport, airtime and data, rent or market levy, packaging, mobile money fees and wages. Small costs add up.

*Example: you sell 20 dresses at K250 = K5,000. Fabric and thread cost K2,600, transport K300, data K100, levy K200. Total costs K3,200. Profit K1,800.*

## A simple daily record
In a notebook or a phone spreadsheet, keep two lists:

- **Money in:** date, what you sold, amount, cash or mobile money.
- **Money out:** date, what you bought or paid, amount.

At the end of each week, add up both and subtract.

## Keep business and personal money apart
Pay yourself a fixed amount instead of taking money from the business whenever you need it. Using a separate business SIM or merchant account makes this easier.

## Stock
Write down what you have and what sells fastest. Buy more of what sells, and less of what does not.

## Use your mobile money statement
Your transaction messages and mini statement already record many payments. Check them against your book.

## Why it matters
Good records help you set the right prices, plan for slow months, apply for a loan and stay on the right side of tax rules.
key_points: Profit is sales minus all costs
Record money in and money out every day
Keep business and personal money separate
lessons.try_it: Write down everything you spent on your business this week, including data and transport.
